title: Le distrait or absentminded beggar
html_source:
This references back to the Scylla and Charybdis episode wherein Stephen is discussing Hamlet, “the distracted” or absentminded beggar. The allusion is to a Hamlet soliloquy in which he asks whether his own inaction is caused by “bestial oblivion,” or by a dull or cowardly thoughtlessness. Since both thought and action in this episode are bestial, “dull” and “cowardly” perhaps are better indictments of Stephen in the previous episode. Hamlet’s tendency to forget his purposes as avenger of his father’s murder, is similar to Stephen’s propensity toward distraction as to his purposes as literary creator, as demonstrated this evening through mind-numbing alcohol and sex, something paralyzing many young Irishmen, but is especially unfortunate with one, who, like Hamlet, has a supposedly unique role to play, requiring action, not degenerate inaction.

Much of Joyce’s great talent is due to a nearly encyclopedic memory and ability to focus, to avoid distraction. Something that becomes very apparent to the Ulysses reader is how critically needful those gifts are for himself.
